questions.question: The First War of Independence (1857) began at which place?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Meerut**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **First War of Independence**, historically referred to as the **Sepoy Mutiny** or the **Rebellion of 1857**, officially began on **May 10, 1857**, in the garrison town of **Meerut**.
 
• The immediate spark for the uprising was the introduction of the **Enfield rifle**, which required soldiers to bite off the ends of cartridges rumored to be greased with **cow and pig fat**, offending both **Hindu** and **Muslim** religious sentiments.
 
• Sepoys of the **3rd Native Cavalry** in **Meerut** refused to use these cartridges, leading to the court-martial and imprisonment of 85 soldiers on **May 9, 1857**.
 
• On the following day, their comrades revolted, killed their British officers, liberated the imprisoned soldiers, and set fire to the **Meerut Cantonment**.
 
• The success of the outbreak in **Meerut** emboldened the troops to march toward the nearby Mughal capital, effectively transforming a military mutiny into a nationwide struggle against the **British East India Company**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Delhi**

 
 
• The mutineers from **Meerut** arrived in **Delhi** on **May 11, 1857**, and proclaimed **Bahadur Shah Zafar** as the **Emperor of Hindustan**.
 
• The city served as the symbolic and political focal point of the rebellion until it was recaptured by the British in **September 1857**.
 
 
 
• **Lucknow**
 
 
• The rebellion in **Lucknow** was led by **Begum Hazrat Mahal**, the wife of the exiled Nawab of **Awadh**, starting in **June 1857**.
 
• It is famous for the **Siege of the Residency**, which lasted for several months before the city was finally cleared by British forces.
 
 
 
• **Kanpur**
 
 
• In **Kanpur**, the revolt was spearheaded by **Nana Sahib**, the adopted son of the last **Peshwa**, **Baji Rao II**.
 
• He was assisted by the military commander **Tantia Tope** and his diplomat **Azimullah Khan** in driving out the British garrison.

questions.question: A solution is prepared by dissolving 15 g of salt in 585 g of water. Calculate the mass percent (w/w) of the solution.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2.5%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mass percent (w/w)** is a measure of the **concentration** of a solute in a solution, representing the mass of the solute per 100 units of the total mass of the solution.
 
• The **mass of the solute** (salt) in this specific problem is provided as **15 g**.
 
• The **mass of the solvent** (water) is provided as **585 g**.
 
• The total **mass of the solution** is the sum of the mass of the solute and the mass of the solvent, which is 15 g + 585 g = **600 g**.
 
• To calculate the **mass percent**, the formula used is: (Mass of solute / Total mass of solution) × 100.
 
• Applying the values to the formula: (15 / 600) × 100. This simplifies to 1500 / 600, which equals **2.5%**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Solute and Solvent**:

 
 
• The **solute** is the substance being dissolved (usually present in a smaller amount), while the **solvent** is the medium doing the dissolving (usually present in a larger amount).
 
• In aqueous solutions, **water** is almost always the solvent due to its polar nature and ability to dissolve many substances.
 
 
 
• **Solution Characteristics**:
 
 
• A solution is a **homogeneous mixture** where the particles of the solute are evenly distributed at the molecular level throughout the solvent.
 
• The **law of conservation of mass** applies here, meaning the mass of the resulting solution is exactly equal to the sum of the masses of the components added.
 
 
 
• **Concentration Units**:
 
 
• Apart from **mass percentage (w/w)**, other common expressions include **volume percentage (v/v)**, **mass by volume percentage (w/v)**, **molarity**, and **parts per million (ppm)**.
 
• Mass percentage is particularly useful in industrial chemical applications where temperature-independent concentration measurements are required.

questions.question: A disk defragmenter rearranges file fragments on a hard drive for faster access. Why is this tool classified as system software rather than application software?

options.text: It primarily maintains and optimizes storage resources, not domain tasks like writing letters.
It only works on removable media.
It is always visible to the user.
It requires Internet access to run.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It primarily maintains and optimizes storage resources, not domain tasks like writing letters.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **disk defragmenter** is a utility program designed to increase **data access speed** by rearranging files stored on a disk to occupy **contiguous storage locations**, a process known as **defragmentation**.
 
• **System software** is a type of computer program that is designed to run a computer's **hardware** and **application programs**; it provides the platform upon which other software operates.
 
• The classification of a defragmenter as **system software** stems from its fundamental role in **resource management** and **hardware optimization**, rather than performing user-centric **domain tasks** like data entry or image editing.
 
• Unlike application software, which serves the user's specific needs, **utility software** like defragmenters serves the needs of the **computer system** itself to ensure efficient **performance** and **stability**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **System Software Categories**:

 
 
• **Operating Systems (OS)**: Examples include **Windows**, **macOS**, and **Linux**, which manage **CPU scheduling** and **memory allocation**.
 
• **Device Drivers**: Specialized programs that allow the **OS** to communicate with hardware like **printers** or **graphics cards**.
 
• **Utility Software**: Tools like **antivirus programs**, **backup software**, and **disk cleaners** that maintain the system.
 
 
 
• **Application Software Characteristics**:
 
 
• Designed for **end-users** to perform specific tasks such as **word processing** (e.g., **MS Word**), **web browsing** (e.g., **Chrome**), or **accounting**.
 
• They rely on the underlying **system software** to interact with **hardware resources**.

questions.question: Which of the following islands of India is closest to the Malabar Coast?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lakshadweep**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Lakshadweep** is an archipelago located in the **Arabian Sea** and is the closest group of islands to the **Malabar Coast** of India.
 
• It is situated at a distance of approximately **220 km** to **440 km** from the coastal city of **Kochi** in **Kerala**.
 
• The **Union Territory** consists of **36 islands**, of which only **10** are inhabited, including **Kavaratti**, **Agatti**, and **Minicoy**.
 
• These islands are unique for being of **coral origin** (atolls), and they are considered a northward extension of the **Chagos-Laccadive Ridge**.
 
• Due to its proximity to the **Malabar Coast**, the islands share deep cultural, linguistic, and historical ties with the state of **Kerala**, with **Malayalam** being the most widely spoken language.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**:

 
 
• Located in the **Bay of Bengal**, these islands are significantly farther from the **Malabar Coast** (which is on the western side of India).
 
• They are separated from the **Indonesian** archipelago by the **Great Channel** and from **Myanmar** by the **Preparis Channel**.
 
 
 
• **Diu Island**:
 
 
• This is a small island located off the southern coast of the **Kathiawar Peninsula** in **Gujarat**.
 
• While it is on the western coast, it is far to the north of the **Malabar Coast**, which primarily covers the **Kerala** shoreline.
 
 
 
• **Malabar Coast**:
 
 
• It represents the southwestern coastline of the **Indian Peninsula**, extending from **Goa** to **Kanyakumari**.
 
• It is famous for its **backwaters** (Kayals) and historically served as a major hub for the international **spice trade**.

questions.question: What is a unitary feature of the Constitution of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Integrated judiciary**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indian Constitution** is described as **quasi-federal** in nature, meaning it contains both **federal** and **unitary** features.
 
• An **Integrated Judiciary** refers to a single system of courts that enforces both **Central laws** and **State laws**. In this hierarchy, the **Supreme Court of India** stands at the apex, followed by **High Courts** in the states and **Subordinate Courts** at the district level.
 
• This system contrasts with a pure federal system (like in the **United States**), where there is a **dual system of courts**: one for federal laws and another for state laws.
 
• The integrated nature ensures **uniformity** in the administration of justice across the entire territory of India, which is a hallmark of a **unitary state**.
 
• Under this structure, the **Supreme Court** has supervisory and appellate jurisdiction over all other courts in the country, reinforcing **centralized judicial control**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Federal Features** of the Indian Constitution:

 
 
• **Bicameral legislature**: The existence of two houses, the **Lok Sabha** (representing the people) and the **Rajya Sabha** (representing the states), is a federal feature ensuring **representation of states** at the center.
 
• **Dual government**: The establishment of governments at both the **Union** and **State** levels with specific jurisdictions is a core federal characteristic.
 
• **Supremacy of the Constitution**: This ensures that both the Center and the States are bound by the **Constitution**, and neither can unilaterally alter the basic structure or division of powers.
 
• **Independent Judiciary**: While the judiciary is integrated (unitary), its **independence** from the executive and legislature is a federal necessity to settle disputes between the Center and States.
 
 
 
• Other **Unitary Features** include:
 
 
• **Single Constitution** for both Union and States.
 
• **Single Citizenship** for all citizens regardless of their state of residence.
 
• **Appointment of the Governor** by the President of India.
 
• **All-India Services** (IAS, IPS, etc.) where officers are recruited by the Center but serve in the States.

questions.question: Which Indian ruler was the first to enter into a Subsidiary Alliance with the British in 1798?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nizam of Hyderabad**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Subsidiary Alliance** was a landmark diplomatic and military policy introduced by **Lord Richard Wellesley**, who served as the **Governor-General of India** from 1798 to 1805.
 
• The **Nizam of Hyderabad** (Nizam Ali Khan) was the first Indian ruler to formally accept the terms of the Subsidiary Alliance in **September 1798**.
 
• Under this treaty, the Nizam was compelled to disband his **French-trained battalions** and replace them with a permanent **British subsidiary force**.
 
• The Nizam agreed to pay for the maintenance of these troops and accepted a **British Resident** at his court, effectively surrendering his **external sovereignty** and foreign relations to the **British East India Company**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The alliance system was designed to eliminate **European rivals** (specifically the **French**) and bring Indian princely states under British **paramountcy**.
 
• Several other major Indian powers were forced into this system over the following years:
 
 
• **Maharaja of Mysore**: Following the fall of Seringapatam and the death of **Tipu Sultan** in the **Fourth Anglo-Mysore War** (1799), the **Wodeyar** dynasty was restored and forced to sign the alliance.
 
• **Nawab of Oudh**: Saadat Ali Khan II was pressured into the Subsidiary Alliance in **November 1801**, ceding substantial territories like **Rohilkhand** and the **Lower Doab** to the Company.
 
• **Peshwa Baji Rao II**: The Marathas entered the fold after the **Peshwa** signed the **Treaty of Bassein** in **1802**.
 
• **Maharaja of Jaipur**: The Rajput states, including **Jaipur**, **Jodhpur**, and **Udaipur**, signed similar treaties much later, predominantly between **1817 and 1818**, during the tenure of **Lord Hastings**.

questions.question: The basic unit of memory used by a computer to store binary data is called a:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bit**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Bit**, which is a portmanteau of **Binary Digit**, represents the smallest possible unit of data and memory in a digital computer or communication system.
 
• It functions as a **logical state** that can only hold one of two values: **0** or **1**. These values typically represent binary conditions such as **Off/On**, **False/True**, or **Low/High** voltage levels.
 
• All complex data types, including text, images, and executable programs, are ultimately stored and processed as long sequences of **bits**.
 
• In **hardware**, bits are physically stored using **capacitors** (charge/no charge), **transistors** (conducting/non-conducting), or **magnetic polarity** on storage disks.
 
• The concept of the bit was pioneered by **Claude Shannon** in 1948, forming the basis of modern **Information Theory** and digital electronics.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Byte**:

 
 
• A **Byte** is a sequence of exactly **8 bits** and is considered the standard unit of addressable memory.
 
• It is used to represent a single **alphanumeric character** in encoding schemes like **ASCII** or **EBCDIC**.
 
 
 
• **Nibble**:
 
 
• A **Nibble** consists of **4 bits**, which is equivalent to half of a standard byte.
 
• This unit is frequently utilized in **microcontroller** programming and to represent a single **hexadecimal** digit (0-F).
 
 
 
• **Word**:
 
 
• A **Word** is the natural unit of data used by a computer **CPU**, representing the number of bits processed in a single cycle.
 
• Common word sizes in modern **computer architecture** include **32-bit** and **64-bit** configurations, which dictate the processing power and memory capacity of the system.

questions.question: What is the first phase of Kerala's Motor Vehicle Department (MVD) child safety rule implementation conducted in October 2024?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Social media awareness campaign**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Kerala **Motor Vehicle Department (MVD)** initiated a phased implementation of stringent child safety regulations beginning in **October 2024** to ensure compliance with the **Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act**.
 
• The first phase was strategically designed as a **social media awareness campaign** to educate the public, especially parents and guardians, about the legal requirements for child safety while traveling.
 
• This phase focused on disseminating information through platforms like **Facebook**, **Instagram**, and **WhatsApp**, highlighting the critical importance of **helmets** for children on two-wheelers and **Child Restraint Systems (CRS)** in four-wheelers.
 
• The objective of starting with an awareness drive was to ensure that citizens were well-informed about the safety standards and potential risks before the department transitioned to stricter **enforcement** and **penalties**.
 
• The campaign specifically targeted the reduction of **pediatric road fatalities** by explaining the technical specifications of safety gear suitable for different age groups.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Child Restraint Systems (CRS)**:

 
 
• These are specialized seats or equipment designed to protect children from injury during **vehicle collisions** or sudden braking.
 
• Under the **Central Motor Vehicles Rules**, children below the age of **12 years** are required to be secured with a **seatbelt** or a **CRS** appropriate for their weight and height.
 
 
 
• **Two-Wheeler Safety for Children**:
 
 
• According to the **Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH)**, children above **9 months** must wear a **crash helmet** of **BIS standard** when riding on a motorcycle.
 
• The speed of the motorcycle carrying a child below **4 years** must not exceed **40 kmph**.
 
 
 
• **Section 194B of the MV Act**:
 
 
• This section stipulates penalties for failing to secure children with safety belts or restraint systems, aiming to enforce the **Safety of Children** clause introduced in the 2019 amendment.
 
 
 
• **Phased Enforcement Strategy**:
 
 
• Modern traffic management in Kerala often follows a **Three-Tier approach**: initial **Public Awareness**, followed by **Stopping and Warning** (Phase 2), and concluding with **Financial Penalties** and **License Suspension** (Phase 3).

questions.question: In a population pyramid, a narrow base and a wider top are most likely to indicate which of the following?

options.text: High birth rates and low death rates
Low birth rates and high life expectancy
Low birth rates and low life expectancy
High birth rates and high death rates

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Low birth rates and high life expectancy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A population pyramid, also known as an **age-sex pyramid**, is a graphical illustration that shows the distribution of various age groups in a population. A **narrow base** indicates that the proportion of children and infants is relatively small, which is a direct consequence of **low birth rates**.
 
• A **wider top** or an apex that remains broad into the upper age brackets signifies that a significant portion of the population survives into old age. This structural feature is the primary indicator of **high life expectancy** and **low geriatric mortality**.
 
• This specific shape is characteristic of a **constrictive pyramid**. It represents a population that is **aging** and may eventually face a natural decrease if birth rates remain below the **replacement level** (typically 2.1 children per woman).
 
• Such demographic profiles are most commonly found in **developed countries** that have completed the **Demographic Transition Model**. Examples include nations like **Japan**, **Germany**, and **Italy**, where healthcare and socio-economic stability support longevity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Types of Population Pyramids:
 
 
• **Expansive Pyramid**:

 
 
• Features a very **wide base** and a **narrow top**.
 
• Indicates **high birth rates** and **high death rates** (or short life expectancy).
 
• Common in **developing nations** with high fertility and limited healthcare access.
 
 
 
• **Stationary Pyramid**:
 
 
• Displays somewhat equal proportions across most age groups, tapering only at the very top.
 
• Reflects stable **birth rates** and **death rates**, often seen in countries like the **United States** or **Australia**.
 
 
 
• **Dependency Ratio**:
 
 
• In a pyramid with a narrow base and wide top, the **old-age dependency ratio** increases.
 
• This places economic pressure on the **working-age population** (typically ages 15 to 64) to support social security and healthcare for the elderly.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most important port-based industrial region in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hooghly industrial belt**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Hooghly industrial belt** is recognized as the most prominent **port-based industrial region** in India, extending along the banks of the **Hooghly River** for about 100 km from **Bansberia** to **Birlapur**.
 
• The region owes its industrial dominance to the **Kolkata Port** and the **Haldia Dock Complex**, which provide vital maritime access for the **import of raw materials** and the **export of finished products** to international markets.
 
• Historically, the belt developed as a major center during the **colonial era**, specifically after the opening of the first **jute mill** at **Rishra** in **1855**, supported by **British capital**.
 
• It is the world’s leading hub for **jute manufacturing** and houses a diverse range of industries including **heavy engineering**, **chemicals**, **pharmaceuticals**, **cotton textiles**, **paper**, and **leather goods**.
 
• The belt benefits from the geographical advantage of being close to the **Chotanagpur Plateau**, ensuring a consistent supply of **coal**, **iron ore**, and other minerals, while the river serves as a source of **cheap inland water transport**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hyderabad-Bengaluru corridor**:

 
 
• This region is primarily a **knowledge-based industrial hub** rather than a port-based one.
 
• It is famous for **Information Technology (IT)**, **Biotechnology**, **Aerospace**, and **Precision Engineering** sectors.
 
 
 
• **Ahmedabad-Vadodara region**:
 
 
• Located in **Gujarat**, this region is a major center for **cotton textiles** and **petrochemicals**.
 
• While it utilizes nearby ports like **Kandla** and **Mundra**, its industrial core is historically rooted in **local cotton production**.
 
 
 
• **Chotanagpur plateau region**:
 
 
• Known as the **mineral heartland** or the **Ruhr of India**, spanning across **Jharkhand**, **West Bengal**, and **Odisha**.
 
• It is an **inland industrial region** focused on **iron and steel** and **metallurgical industries** due to vast deposits of **coal** and **metallic minerals**.

questions.question: How did Sayyid Ahmad Khan’s Aligarh Movement differ from the Arya Samaj?

options.text: Aligarh Movement rejected modern learning, while Arya Samaj discouraged rational thinking.
Aligarh Movement supported Western-style education, while Arya Samaj promoted Vedic studies.
Aligarh Movement encouraged priestly control, while Arya Samaj rejected monotheism.
Aligarh Movement opposed science, while Arya Samaj rejected old scriptures.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aligarh Movement supported Western-style education, while Arya Samaj promoted Vedic studies.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Aligarh Movement**, led by **Sir Sayyid Ahmad Khan**, primarily aimed at the social and educational advancement of Indian Muslims by reconciling **Islamic teachings** with **modern Western education** and **scientific temperament**.
 
• The movement established the **Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College** in **1875** at **Aligarh**, which later became the **Aligarh Muslim University**, focusing on **English literature** and **physical sciences**.
 
• In contrast, the **Arya Samaj**, founded by **Swami Dayanand Saraswati** in **1875**, was a **revivalist movement** that sought to reform **Hinduism** by returning to the original teachings of the **Vedas**.
 
• The core philosophy of **Arya Samaj** was captured in the slogan **Back to the Vedas**, emphasizing **Vedic studies**, **monotheism**, and the rejection of **idol worship** and **ritualistic priesthood**.
 
• While both movements advocated for **social reform** (such as women’s education and the removal of social evils), their academic foundations differed significantly: one looked toward the **modern West** for intellectual progress, while the other looked toward **ancient Indian scriptures**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sir Sayyid Ahmad Khan**:

 
 
• He authored the journal **Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq** to spread awareness about **social reforms** and **rationalism**.
 
• He believed that the **Muslim community** could only progress by cooperating with the **British administration** and mastering **Western sciences**.
 
 
 
• **Swami Dayanand Saraswati**:
 
 
• His famous work, **Satyarth Prakash** (The Light of Truth), detailed his interpretations of the **Vedas** and criticized later **Puranic** distortions.
 
• The **Arya Samaj** also introduced the **Shuddhi movement** to bring individuals back into the Hindu fold, which marked a shift toward **organized proselytization**.
 
 
 
• **Educational Legacy**:
 
 
• The **Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV)** schools were a later compromise that integrated **Vedic education** with **modern curriculum**, whereas the **Aligarh Movement** remained the standard-bearer for **Western-style higher education** in the 19th century.

questions.question: Starch, a major component of flour and potatoes, is a **polysaccharide**. What chemical process occurs when starch is heated with water?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gelatinization**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gelatinization** is a biochemical process that occurs when **starch granules** are heated in the presence of **water**, causing the granules to absorb moisture and swell significantly.
 
• Starch consists of two types of **polysaccharide** molecules: **Amylose** (linear) and **Amylopectin** (branched). During heating, the **hydrogen bonds** between these molecules are weakened, allowing water to enter the granule.
 
• As water is absorbed, the **crystalline structure** of the starch is disrupted, leading to the leaching of **Amylose** into the surrounding liquid, which results in an increase in **viscosity** and the formation of a **starch paste**.
 
• The temperature at which this process begins is known as the **gelatinization temperature**, which typically ranges from **60°C to 75°C** for most common food starches like those found in **flour** and **potatoes**.
 
• This phenomenon is crucial in cooking for thickening **soups**, **sauces**, and providing the characteristic texture to boiled **potatoes** and baked **bread**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Saponification**

 
 
• This is a chemical reaction between a **fat or oil** (triglyceride) and a strong **alkali** (such as **Sodium Hydroxide** or Potassium Hydroxide) to produce **soap** and **glycerol**.
 
 
 
• **Caramelization**

questions.question: The zone on Earth where no S-waves are detected is known as:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Shadow zone**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• An earthquake **Shadow Zone** refers to the specific region on the **Earth** surface where **seismographs** are unable to detect **seismic waves** from a particular **epicenter**.
 
• **Secondary waves (S-waves)** are transverse **body waves** that can only propagate through **solid media**; they possess no **shear strength** to pass through **fluids** like **liquids** or **gases**.
 
• The **Earth** structure includes a **liquid outer core**, which begins at the **Gutenberg Discontinuity** at a depth of approximately **2,900 kilometers**.
 
• Because **S-waves** cannot travel through the **liquid outer core**, they are completely blocked, creating a massive **shadow zone** that extends from an angular distance of **103 degrees** to **180 degrees** from the **epicenter**.
 
• The **S-wave shadow zone** is significantly larger than the **P-wave shadow zone**, covering nearly **40 percent** of the entire **Earth** surface.
 
• The existence of this zone provided scientists like **Richard Dixon Oldham** and **Inge Lehmann** with the primary evidence that the **Earth** has a **liquid core**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Seismic Waves and Barriers**:

 
 
• **P-wave Shadow Zone**: **Primary waves (P-waves)** are longitudinal and can pass through solids and liquids; however, they are **refracted** (bent) at the **core-mantle boundary**, creating a shadow zone between **103 degrees** and **142 degrees** from the **epicenter**.
 
• **Seismic Belt**: This refers to elongated regions of high **seismic activity**, such as the **Alpide belt** or the **Circum-Pacific Belt** (Ring of Fire), where **plate boundaries** frequently generate **earthquakes**.
 
• **Epicentral Gap**: Also known as a **seismic gap**, this is a segment of an active **tectonic fault** that has not slipped in a long time compared to other segments, indicating a high probability of a future **major earthquake**.
 
• **Active Zone**: Geologically unstable regions characterized by frequent **tectonic movements**, **volcanism**, and **seismic energy** release.

• The operation relies on the **Clipboard**, a temporary storage buffer in the computer's **Random Access Memory (RAM)** that holds data retrieved via the **Copy (Ctrl + C)** or **Cut (Ctrl + X)** commands.
 
• In **macOS**, the equivalent functional shortcut is **Command + V**, but across **Windows** and **Linux** distributions, **Ctrl + V** remains the standard for text editors, web browsers, and file management systems.
 
• When used, it identifies the **insertion point** (cursor position) and replicates the data format (if supported) such as **plain text**, **rich text**, or **embedded objects**.

• This is the **Save** shortcut used to write the current data of an application from the volatile **RAM** to a non-volatile **storage device** like an **SSD** or **HDD**.

questions.question: What is the approximate speed of sound in air at room temperature (approximately 20°C)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**343 m/s**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The speed of sound is defined as the distance traveled per unit of time by a sound wave as it propagates through an elastic medium. In air, sound is a **longitudinal wave** that moves through a series of **compressions** and **rarefactions**.
 
• The speed of sound in a medium depends primarily on the **elasticity** and **density** of that medium. In the case of gases, the **temperature** is the most critical variable affecting speed.
 
• At a standard temperature of **0°C** (273 K), the speed of sound in dry air is approximately **331.5 m/s**.
 
• As the temperature of the air increases, the kinetic energy of the molecules increases, allowing the sound vibration to be transmitted more rapidly. The relationship is expressed by the approximate formula: v = 331.5 + 0.6 × T, where T represents the temperature in **degrees Celsius**.
 
• For a typical **room temperature** of **20°C**, the calculation is v = 331.5 + (0.6 × 20), resulting in **343.5 m/s**. Consequently, **343 m/s** is recognized as the standard approximate value for sound speed at this temperature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Speed of sound in various media:
 
 
• **Solids**: Sound travels fastest in solids because the particles are very close together. In **Steel**, the speed is approximately **5960 m/s**, and in **Aluminum**, it reaches about **6420 m/s**.
 
• **Liquids**: Sound travels faster in liquids than in gases but slower than in solids. In **distilled water** at 20°C, the speed is roughly **1482 m/s**, while in **Seawater**, it is approximately **1531 m/s**.
 
• **Gases**: Sound travels slowest in gases. For example, in **Helium** at 0°C, the speed is about **965 m/s**, which is faster than in air due to helium's lower density.
 
 
 
• Environmental Factors:
 
 
• **Humidity**: Increased humidity leads to a slight increase in the speed of sound because water vapor is less dense than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules it replaces in the air.
 
• **Pressure**: In an ideal gas, the speed of sound is **independent of pressure** as long as the temperature remains constant.

questions.question: The Fundamental Duties suggested by the Swaran Singh Committee were incorporated through which Constitutional Amendment?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**42ⁿd Amendment**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Fundamental Duties** were incorporated into the **Indian Constitution** following the recommendations of the **Swaran Singh Committee**, which was established by the government in **1976**.
 
• The committee suggested that a separate chapter on fundamental duties be added to ensure that citizens are aware of their obligations while enjoying their **Fundamental Rights**, particularly during the **National Emergency**.
 
• Based on these suggestions, the **42ⁿd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976** was enacted, which introduced a new **Part IV-A** and a single new **Article 51A** to the Constitution.
 
• Initially, the committee recommended the inclusion of **eight fundamental duties**; however, the **42ⁿd Amendment** actually included **ten duties**.
 
• The recommendations included a provision for **Parliament** to impose penalties for non-compliance, but this specific suggestion was not accepted and thus not included in the final amendment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **44th Amendment Act, 1978**:

 
 
• This amendment was passed by the **Janata Government** to undo several changes made during the **Emergency**.
 
• It famously stripped the **Right to Property** of its status as a **Fundamental Right** and made it a legal right under **Article 300A**.
 
 
 
• **86th Amendment Act, 2002**:
 
 
• This amendment added the **11th Fundamental Duty** to the existing list, which pertains to providing educational opportunities to children aged **6 to 14 years**.
 
• It also established the **Right to Education** as a **Fundamental Right** under **Article 21A**.
 
 
 
• **Other Amendments**:
 
 
• The **40th Amendment Act, 1976** empowered **Parliament** to define the limits of **India's territorial waters** and the **Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ)**.
 
• The **48th Amendment Act, 1984** was specifically concerned with the extension of **President’s Rule** in the state of **Punjab**.
 
 
 
• **Origins**:
 
 
• The concept of Fundamental Duties in India was inspired by the Constitution of the former **USSR**.
 
• These duties are **non-justiciable** in nature, meaning they cannot be directly enforced by the courts through writs.

• Sound is a **mechanical longitudinal wave** that requires a material medium to propagate, traveling through the periodic compression and rarefaction of particles.
 
• The speed of sound depends on the **elasticity** and **density** of the medium. It is mathematically represented as the square root of the ratio of the **elastic modulus** to the **inertial density**.
 
• In **solids**, atoms are more closely packed and bound by stronger **intermolecular forces** compared to liquids or gases. This high **elasticity** allows the vibrational energy to be transferred much more efficiently and rapidly between adjacent atoms.
 
• Among the given options, **Iron** is a solid with a high **stiffness** (Young's modulus). Consequently, sound travels fastest through it at a speed of approximately **5,130 m/s** at room temperature.
 
• As a general rule, the speed of sound follows the order: **Solids > Liquids > Gases**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Air**

 
 
• It is a **gaseous medium** where molecules are widely separated and interact weakly.
 
• The speed of sound in air is relatively slow, measured at approximately **343 m/s** at a standard temperature of **20°C**.
 
 
 
• **Water**
 
 
• As a **liquid**, it is less compressible than air but far more compressible than solids.
 
• Sound travels at an intermediate speed in water, roughly **1,480 m/s**, which is about four times faster than in air but significantly slower than in metals.
 
 
 
• **Vacuum**
 
 
• A vacuum is a space devoid of matter. Since sound is a **mechanical wave** that relies on particle-to-particle interaction, it cannot propagate in a **vacuum**.
 
• The speed of sound in a vacuum is **zero**.

questions.solution:

• **Population density** is a geographical measurement of the number of people residing within a specific region relative to its size, typically expressed as people per **unit of land area**, such as a **square kilometer** or **square mile**.
 
• The most common method of calculation is **Arithmetic Density**, which is derived by dividing the **total population** of a country or region by its **total land area** in square units.
 
• According to the **2011 Census of India**, the national population density was recorded at **382 persons per square kilometer**, reflecting a steady increase from **324 persons per square kilometer** in 2001.
 
• This metric serves as a vital tool for **demographers** and **urban planners** to assess the **carrying capacity** of land, plan **infrastructure development**, and determine the distribution of **public services**.

questions.question: What is the meaning of globalisation?

options.text: Reduction in the volume of international trade
Expansion of state ownership across major industries
Economic isolation of countries from global markets
Integration of a country’s economy with the world economy

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Integration of a country’s economy with the world economy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Globalisation** is defined as the process of rapid **integration** or interconnection between countries through the increased flow of goods, services, investments, and people across international borders.
 
• It involves the **opening up** of domestic markets to foreign players and the removal of various **trade barriers**, such as tariffs and quotas, to facilitate a seamless exchange in the **global market**.
 
• The process is significantly driven by advancements in **Information and Communication Technology (ICT)** and transport, which have made the physical distance between countries less relevant for economic activities.
 
• In **India**, globalisation became a cornerstone of the **New Economic Policy (NEP)** launched in **July 1991**, shifting the nation away from a closed economy toward an outward-oriented economic framework.
 
• **Multinational Corporations (MNCs)** play a pivotal role in this process by setting up production units and offices in multiple countries, thereby linking disparate economies through **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Globalisation is often discussed alongside two other core concepts of the **1991 Reforms**:

 
 
• **Liberalisation**: The policy of reducing or eliminating government regulations and restrictions on private business and industry to encourage competition.
 
• **Privatisation**: The transfer of ownership, management, and control of **Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)** to the private sector to improve efficiency.
 
 
 
• **World Trade Organization (WTO)**: Established in **1995**, this international body oversees the rules of trade between nations and works toward the liberalisation of global trade.
 
• **Outsourcing**: An important outcome of globalisation where companies delegate business processes (like **BPOs**) to external providers in countries with lower costs, such as **India**.
 
• The concepts of **Economic Isolation** or **Autarky** are the direct opposites of globalisation, where a country avoids international trade and aims for self-sufficiency.

questions.question: *Karagattam, a popular folk dance of Tamil Nadu performed mainly by women balancing decorated pots, is dedicated to which deity?*

• The dance is traditionally dedicated to **Goddess Mariamman**, who is revered in South Indian tradition as the **Goddess of Rain** and the protector against infectious diseases like smallpox and cholera.
 
• The performance is deeply rooted in **Dravidian culture** and is typically held during temple festivals, especially in the Tamil month of **Aadi**, to invoke the goddess for a bountiful harvest and rainfall.
 
• There are two main variants of this dance: **Sakthi Karagam**, which is performed strictly within temple premises for religious rituals, and **Atta Karagam**, which is a more theatrical version performed for public entertainment.
 
• The **Karagam** pot is usually made of mud, bronze, or brass and is filled with **uncooked rice** or water to provide the necessary weight for balance; it is topped with a conical arrangement of flowers and a wooden or paper **parrot**.
 
• Dancers perform to the rhythmic beats of the **Naiyandi Melam**, which includes instruments like the **Thavil**, **Pambai**, and **Urumi**, showcasing extraordinary physical coordination and balance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Goddess Kamakshi**:

 
 
• She is a form of **Tripura Sundari** or **Parvati** and is the presiding deity of the **Kanchi Kamakshi Amman Temple** in **Kanchipuram**.
 
• She is depicted in a **Padmasana** (yogic) posture, holding a sugarcane bow and floral arrows, representing love and devotion.
 
 
 
• **Goddess Andal**:
 
 
• She is the only female **Alvar** saint among the twelve **Vaishnavite** saints of South India, known for her compositions like **Thiruppavai**.
 
• She is worshipped as an incarnation of **Bhu Devi** (Mother Earth) and is central to the traditions of the **Srivilliputhur** temple.
 
 
 
• **Goddess Meenakshi**:
 
 
• An avatar of **Parvati**, she is the primary deity of the historic **Meenakshi Amman Temple** in **Madurai**.
 
• She is often represented with a **parrot** on her shoulder and is celebrated for her role as the sovereign queen of the **Pandyan** kingdom.
